messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Faris Haddad is a 40-year-old paramedic who came to treatment nearly a year after the call that changed how he understood himself. He had been working a weekend shift when dispatch sent his unit to a highway collision involving a family sedan and a delivery truck. When he reached the scene, he recognized the passenger before he fully registered the wreckage: his younger sister’s husband had been driving, and his sister Layla was in the back seat beside their injured son. There was blood across Layla’s face and neck, glass in her hair, and the chemical smell of fuel mixed with the sharp antiseptic odor from the trauma supplies he tore open with shaking hands. He remembers flashes with terrible clarity—the wet shine of an open wound, Layla looking at him and saying his name, his nephew crying—and other parts are missing altogether. He cannot piece together exactly when he moved from the truck to the car, or the sequence of what he said. What does return comes back with the same terror he felt there, not as a story but as something happening again in full sensory detail.

In the weeks afterward, Faris had come to believe that this memory proved something devastating about him. He was certain he had failed in the one situation in which being a paramedic and a brother should have meant he could protect his family. The blank spots in his memory tormented him; because he could not account for everything he had done, he took the gaps as evidence that he could not rely on himself when it mattered most. Each reliving left him feeling permanently altered, as if the competent version of himself had been replaced by someone weaker and less dependable. Those conclusions sharpened what caught his attention. On shift, visible injuries on patients no longer looked like routine parts of the job but like accusations, and even passing the ambulance bay sink when it smelled of antiseptic could make his body brace before he had consciously placed why.

Those reminders quickly began pulling him back into the crash. A scalp laceration on a patient, a child mentioning his mother, the hospital-clean smell in an emergency department could make the scene with Layla surge up as fully real, with the same sensory force and panic. At work he would lose track of report details midway through listening, because his concentration narrowed around the feeling that something awful was about to happen again. He startled violently if a colleague touched his shoulder from behind, and in break rooms or waiting areas he automatically chose the chair with the clearest view of the door and the most protected position against the wall. As he became more keyed up, he noticed more reminders everywhere: every wound looked too much like that night, every victim’s face risked turning into his sister’s, every medicinal smell seemed to announce another disaster.

Faris responded by trying not to think about the crash at all. He would clamp down on images, push away Layla’s voice, and tell himself to stay focused on tasks. On days off he found excuses to pick up errands or projects around the house simply to keep his mind occupied, and when he could not avoid work altogether he overworked within it—restocking excessively, volunteering for extra administrative tasks, burying himself in checklists. Yet the harder he fought the memory, the more abruptly it returned. Suppressing it seemed to make the missing pieces feel even more ominous, and his frantic busyness left him more brittle, more easily startled, and more likely to scan for the next reminder. He began dreading shifts because he knew they exposed him to injured bodies and victim stories, but staying away from work also fed his fear that he was no longer the kind of man who could do his job.

At home, the pattern tightened further. When his wife touched him unexpectedly while he was distracted, he jerked away in alarm and then felt ashamed. That reaction confirmed, in his mind, that he had changed for the worse. The shame pushed him to withdraw into chores or extra shifts rather than talk, and the distance this created in his marriage became one more sign that he was failing people he loved. His constant need to sit facing entrances in restaurants or family gatherings embarrassed him, but he felt he had to stay prepared. Living that way kept him on edge, and being on edge made the crash easier to relive and the triggers easier to spot.

He finally sought help after freezing during a pediatric trauma call when the antiseptic smell and the sight of facial injuries brought Layla’s bloodied face back so completely that for a moment he was no longer sure where he was. He finished the call, but afterward he sat in the ambulance unable to concentrate, convinced he could not trust himself and terrified that next time someone would suffer because of him. What he wants most is to be able to go to work, come home to his wife, and remember that night without being dropped back into it; what he fears most is that the man who failed to protect his family is now the only version of him left.
